snippet.title: Why Did Betelgeuse Suddenly Lose Two-Thirds of Its Light?
snippet.description:
Is Betelgeuse About to Explode?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vP1BbqZ_dnM

By February 2020, the red supergiant Betelgeuse on Orion's shoulder had faded to about a third of its usual brightness. Rather than an imminent explosion, a huge bubble of gas had erupted from the star's surface, cooled as it drifted away, and condensed into a cloud of dust that blocked part of Betelgeuse from our view.

Sources: Montargès et al. (2021), Nature 594, 365–368 — the 2019–2020 Great Dimming dust veil and cool photospheric patch (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03546-8) · Dupree et al. (2022), The Astrophysical Journal 936, 18 — the surface mass ejection and 400-day pulsation reset (https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ac7853).

Pictures: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Horálek night-sky starfield (CC BY 4.0), ESO/M. Montargès et al. VLT/SPHERE resolved images of Betelgeuse in January and December 2019 (CC BY 4.0), ESO/P. Kervella VLT/VISIR plume image (CC BY 4.0), and ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser illustrations of Betelgeuse's mass ejection and dust veil (CC BY 4.0), alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Artist's impressions are identified on screen. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Horálek (CC BY 4.0); ESO/M. Montargès et al. (CC BY 4.0); ESO/P. Kervella (CC BY 4.0); ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

snippet.title: Is Betelgeuse Really About to Explode?
snippet.description:
Is Betelgeuse About to Explode?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vP1BbqZ_dnM

The orange star on Orion's shoulder is a dying red supergiant. One day Betelgeuse will blow itself apart as a supernova and shine so brightly for weeks that it will be visible in the daytime sky — but what do the 2019 Great Dimming and seismic models say about when?

Sources: Joyce et al. (2020), The Astrophysical Journal 902, 63 — Betelgeuse radius, mass, distance and core helium-burning stage (https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/abb8db) · Montargès et al. (2021), Nature 594, 365–368 — the 2019–2020 Great Dimming dust veil (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03546-8) · Goldberg, Bauer & Howell (2020), Research Notes of the AAS 4, 35 — Type IIP supernova plateau brightness at half-Moon scale (https://doi.org/10.3847/2515-5172/ab7c68).

Pictures: ESO/B. Tafreshi (twanight.org), R. Wesson/ESO, ESO/S. Brunier, and ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO) Orion and observatory time-lapses (CC BY 4.0), and ESO/M. Montargès et al. VLT/SPHERE image of Betelgeuse (CC BY 4.0), alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: ESO/B. Tafreshi (twanight.org, CC BY 4.0); R. Wesson/ESO (CC BY 4.0); ESO/S. Brunier (CC BY 4.0); ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO, CC BY 4.0); ESO/M. Montargès et al. (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

snippet.title: How Bright Will Betelgeuse Get When It Explodes?
snippet.description:
Is Betelgeuse About to Explode?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vP1BbqZ_dnM

When Betelgeuse's core collapses, the first sign to reach Earth will be a flood of neutrinos hours before the shockwave breaks the star's surface. Within days, Betelgeuse will blaze as bright as the Moon at half phase — bright enough to cast shadows at night and remain visible in broad daylight.

Sources: Goldberg, Bauer & Howell (2020), Research Notes of the AAS 4, 35 — Type IIP supernova plateau brightness at half-Moon scale (https://doi.org/10.3847/2515-5172/ab7c68) · Joyce et al. (2020), The Astrophysical Journal 902, 63 — Betelgeuse radius, mass, distance and evolutionary state (https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/abb8db).

Pictures: NASA/CXC/STScI/JPL-Caltech composite of the Cassiopeia A supernova remnant, ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO) Chajnantor Milky Way time-lapse (CC BY 4.0), NASA/DSCOVR EPIC full-disk Earth image, and NASA Apollo 17 Moon photograph, alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/CXC/STScI/JPL-Caltech; ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO, CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); NASA/DSCOVR EPIC; NASA Apollo 17.
